objective.title: Approach optimal play through robust self-play
objective.summary: The long-term goal is approximate optimal / equilibrium-oriented play in the closed-team-sheet VGC game. Measure progress across held-out teams and a varied opponent set; report average, lower-percentile, and worst-case results. No single opponent or fixed win-rate threshold defines completion.

candidate.label: Current in-battle policy vs Round424 start
candidate.status: Current validated candidate · Round436 ablation and external screens inconclusive
candidate.note: Round431 scored 49.36% [45.85%, 52.93%] against Round430, and Round432 scored 47.90% [44.29%, 51.61%]; neither showed a clear gain. Round430 remains the validated in-battle candidate. Round402's 77.15% result is a separate team-preview selector benchmark. Round432 external screens also showed no clear lift: all paired 95% intervals vs Round430 and Round431 include zero. Round432 cross-opponent equal-weight mean/median/p10/worst were 60.35%/48.83%/47.64%/47.46%; the mean is buoyed by random play. Round435 used a Round434 restricted-game mixture (31.7% Round430 / 68.3% Round432 in the policy pool) and scored 52.98% [49.41%, 56.59%] head-to-head with Round430; all matched external deltas vs Round430/432 included zero. Round430 remains the candidate. Round436 removed hidden-set auxiliary loss on the identical Round435 data; it scored 53.42% [49.80%, 56.93%] vs Round435 over 512 clusters (one incomplete game), an inconclusive ablation. Round430 remains the validated candidate. Round436 external screens at 256 clusters found no supported paired gain vs Round435: deltas on 128 shared clusters were +0.20 pp vs Max Damage [-0.59,+0.98], +0.39 pp vs public Counterplay [-0.59,+1.37], 0.00 pp vs random [-0.78,+0.78], and -0.20 pp vs Round102 [-0.98,+0.39]. Round436 remains unpromoted; Round430 is still the validated candidate. Round462’s latest full training run screened at 44.82% vs Max Damage [41.02%, 48.54%] and around 48% vs Public Counterplay/historical PPO. Do not promote it; the Max Damage interval is below 50% and performance vs stronger policy opponents is inconclusive. Exact-seed Max Damage controls found no measurable change from Round430: +0.10 pp [−1.37, +1.56]; Round432 control was +0.39 pp [−1.37, +2.05]. The weakness predates Round462.

speed.context: Round473: 20,000 fresh hard-opponent games in 520.77 s; input-to-checkpoint in 940.75 s; peak aggregate rollout RSS 9.60 GiB.
speed.decision_latency: 131–204 ms per episode across hard-opponent classes
speed.current_bottleneck: Public Counterplay scoring 77.8 ms; policy-pool inference 70.2 ms; observation encoding 25–29 ms; Showdown engine 29–35 ms per episode.
speed.gpu_status: RTX 4060 used for PPO optimization; rollout decisions and headless simulator remain CPU-side
speed.profile_context: Round467 completed 20,000 rollouts: per-worker speed 7.53/5.34/4.84 games/s for Max Damage/policy/Public Counterplay. PPO preparation took 89 s; the KL-stopped CUDA optimizer ran about 5 s. Aggregate rollout wall time was not retained.

active_training_profile.status: Round473 fresh hard-opponent mixed PPO rollout profile
active_training_profile.context: Per-shard averages. Aggregate rollout was 38.40 games/s over 20,000 matches on eight CPU workers; do not sum per-shard rates.

opportunities.title: 1 · Batch policy inference across live rollouts
opportunities.detail: Historical-policy rollouts spent about 72 ms/match in inference. Workers currently infer independently on CPU. Gather ready decisions from concurrent matches into a shared batch, then compare CPU batching with a single GPU inference service at observed batch sizes. Measure games/s, queue delay, and p95 decision latency before adopting it.

opportunities.title: 2 · Reduce observation encoding work
opportunities.detail: Encoding used about 22–29 ms/match. Precompute static dex/team features, cache repeated derived values, and reuse compact numeric buffers across decisions. Profile each stage and retain the closed-team-sheet leakage audit.

opportunities.title: 3 · Batch rollouts and tune worker count
opportunities.detail: A fixed 240-game Max Damage benchmark measured 30.94 games/s at 8 workers, versus 29.09 at 12 and 26.04 at 16; memory also rose from 6.77 GB at 8 to 13.25 GB at 16. Keep 8 as the measured setting for now. Test batching requests across those workers before increasing concurrency.

opportunities.title: 4 · Reduce counterplay scorer cost
opportunities.detail: A per-decision cache for repeated public damage calculations cut scorer time from 203.4 to 62.6 ms/match (69%) in a paired 32-game single-worker probe. In a separate 240-game, 8-worker run, scoring averaged 80.1 ms/match and aggregate rollout throughput was 23.51 games/s, with no timeouts or corrections. Still compare an 8-worker pre-cache control and rerun the full mixed PPO iteration; then profile repeated speed and legality calculations.

opportunities.title: 5 · Reuse the audited PPO counts and digest
opportunities.detail: A separate sample-count scan over Round435’s 3.87 GiB and 28,000 valid rollout records took 35.96 s (162,366 trainable transitions). The strict audit already reads the data and computes those counts, so the headless PPO path reuses its counts and SHA-256 digest to skip the duplicate pass. An independent recomputation matched the digest and counts exactly. Same-data PPO replay wall time was 217.98 s with reuse vs 260.74 s without (42.77 s / 16.4% faster); both produced bit-identical model parameters and identical metrics across 1,272 steps. These are PPO-update timings without rollout generation. Treat the separately measured 35.96 s scan as the direct saving; the rest of the observed difference is run variation.

opportunities.title: 6 · Trim trajectory persistence
opportunities.detail: Writes used 7–12 ms/match and Round424 stored about 1.8 GB for 10,000 games. Benchmark buffered compact records or chunk compression after the higher-cost action and inference paths.

opportunities.title: 7 · Keep CPU inference eager; profile feature/scorer cost
opportunities.detail: Round452 completed the full-match check of torch.compile: 13.15 games/s eager vs 4.30 compiled at eight workers, with policy inference 65.8 vs 944.6 ms/match and peak RSS 6.60 vs 11.67 GiB. Reject compiled inference in rollout workers. The single-state 1.47× gain did not transfer. Focus on feature preparation and public-counterplay scoring; see raw Round452 comparison.

opportunities.title: 8 · Trim per-state PPO input assembly
opportunities.detail: Round453’s NumPy field encoder and Round454’s per-record static team-key reuse both preserve exact model-input tensors. Their isolated input-builder reductions were 7.07% and 10.75%, respectively. Round454’s full 20k-game PPO replay matched all metrics/checkpoint tensors but had 163.68 s preparation vs Round453’s 163.07 s, so the isolated gain did not produce a further measurable full-update reduction. Complete-iteration rate remains 16.49 games/s.

opportunities.title: 9 · Profile public-mechanics and transition extraction
opportunities.detail: Rounds455–457 cached public-mechanics facts, optimized encoder loops, and reduced repeated validation work. The reader benchmark improved 5.99% on 1,024 audited rows and extraction 4.19% on 1,971 transitions, both with exact output parity. Matched PPO replays ranged 158.25–161.40 s for preparation and 223.76–226.59 s wall, so small end-to-end speed gains remain unresolved. Next profile complete sample-preparation chunks to separate JSON validation, transition extraction, and model-input construction.

speed.jax_decision: Round430 confirms the Showdown engine used about 18% of policy-pool match time and 8% against Public Counterplay; a simulator-only port would leave the larger measured policy, observation, and baseline-scoring costs intact. Keep Showdown as the correctness reference and require an end-to-end measured gain before a JAX/GPU engine prototype.
speed.remaining_summary: Round462 attributes 30.4 ms/episode telemetry to the Showdown roundtrip (~15%); the remaining time is dominated by action selection (81.8 ms), observation encoding (27.2 ms), trajectory persistence (20.1 ms), and setup/other work. Policy inference and baseline scoring are already included inside action selection.

remaining_components.note: Includes 73.1 ms policy inference; do not add inference again.
Repeated feature construction and static lookups.
Remaining measured episode time after named stages.

speed.worker_scaling_context: Round430 CPU rollout scaling on the 16-logical-CPU host, with 240 complete matches per setting against Max Damage. Eight workers were fastest in this short single-opponent sample; 12 and 16 workers consumed more memory and ran slower. Test batching across the existing workers before increasing worker count.

policy_inference_benchmark.context: Round430 checkpoint on 256 perspective-safe rollout states; 1 CPU thread, 5 warmups, 30 timed repeats. Timings include host-to-device transfer and action/value synchronization; collation is reported separately. Queue wait is excluded.
policy_inference_benchmark.interpretation: CUDA is slower for single states and roughly tied with CPU at batch 8, about 51% faster at batch 16, and 2.6x faster at batch 32. Queue wait is excluded. A scalar-clamp optimization reduced warm native action-feature time 41.3% (0.1983 to 0.1165 ms/state) with exact outputs against the prior NumPy-clamp implementation on 256 inputs; whole-match speed impact is not yet measured.
policy_inference_benchmark.feature_replay_caveat: The initial Round430 parity audit used initial-team opponent ordering and PPO's conditionally narrowed action mask, unlike live feature generation. New rollout data now saves per-step opponent preview order, the raw feature mask, the PPO conditional mask, and encoder version. On a fresh 64-game rollout (128 perspective records, 481 feature states), recomputation matched every saved feature value exactly. Legacy Round430 records remain missing the raw action mask, but PPO continues to train from the saved feature arrays.

counterplay_cache_benchmark.context: Same Round430 checkpoint, VGC format, 32 episode seeds, one CPU worker, and /dev/null trajectory output before and after memoizing repeated deterministic damage estimates within each joint-action score. This is a microbenchmark, not the standard 8-worker mixed-training run.
counterplay_cache_benchmark.result: Both runs produced 13 Headless P1 wins and 19 Headless P2 wins, with 0 timeouts and 0 action corrections. Policy inference averaged 31.9 vs 31.4 ms/match, observation encoding 19.5 vs 19.1 ms, and engine roundtrips 29.2 vs 28.1 ms.
counterplay_cache_benchmark.limitation: The 32-game before/after is paired on identical seeds. The 8-worker rollout validates concurrent operation but has no pre-cache 8-worker control; full 20,000-game mixed PPO throughput has not yet been remeasured.

cpu_inference_followups.context: Round450 and Round451 used the Round447 checkpoint and 256 real closed-sheet Round435 states; measurements cover full native action selection but are microbenchmarks, not complete matches.

compiled_policy.status: Rejected for rollout use: the full-match run was slower despite exact action parity in the earlier microbenchmark.

dynamic_int8.status: Rejected for now: slower and 1.95% action disagreement.

cpu_inference_followups.next_step: Keep eager CPU inference. The matched eight-worker Round452 full-match run measured 13.15 games/s eager vs 4.30 compiled; policy inference was 65.8 vs 944.6 ms/match, and peak RSS was 6.60 vs 11.67 GiB. Focus next on observation/action feature preparation and public-counterplay scoring; only revisit compilation after explaining repeated compile/runtime overhead.

full_match_compile_benchmark.context: Round452 compared eager and torch.compile CPU inference on the Round430 checkpoint with the same seed, episode offsets, eight workers, and Max Damage opponent; 64 complete matches per condition. Includes process startup and compilation.
full_match_compile_benchmark.finding: The single-state torch.compile advantage did not transfer to rollout workers. Cold eight-worker complete-match throughput fell from 13.15 to 4.30 games/s; measured policy inference rose from about 65.8 to 944.6 ms/match and peak RSS rose from 6.60 to 11.67 GiB. Keep compilation disabled for training. This small run is a speed comparison, not a strength evaluation.
full_match_compile_benchmark.limitations: Each condition ran 64 matches and included process startup and compilation. Same seeds and episode offsets were used; policy action sampling and game randomness mean match outcomes are not a powered strength comparison. Test set was a short Max Damage workload, not the full opponent mixture.

ppo_preparation_optimization.context: Round447 prepared 162,366 transitions from 20,000 games in 169.12 s; full replay was about 232 s and matched Round437 checkpoint tensors exactly. Round453 optimized one measured input-encoding substage; current 16.49 games/s complete training-iteration baseline remains Round430.
ppo_preparation_optimization.scope_note: 1,026 real states, seven repeats after warm-up. Linear extrapolation only; no full PPO replay has measured the net change yet.
ppo_preparation_optimization.matched_replay_context: The complete PPO replay preserved all metrics and model tensors. Sample collection was 6.05 s (3.58%) faster than Round447; the whole replay was about 3.36 s faster than Round447 but remains slower than Round437’s 217.98 s. One matched replay cannot separate the code change from run-to-run variance or attribute all observed savings to the NumPy encoder; repeat the matched comparison before claiming reliable end-to-end throughput gain.

static_team_signature_benchmark.context: Round454 moved static own/opponent token-key construction from every state to once per audited player-view record. Opponent key data is public species only.
static_team_signature_benchmark.scope_note: Input construction with cached static token tensors; key construction is done once per record as in NativePPOTrainer. Record parsing, transition extraction and PPO optimization are excluded.

static_team_key_full_replay.context: Full matched PPO replay on Round447 data/config. All metrics and all 82 checkpoint tensors were identical.
static_team_key_full_replay.finding: All 82 final model tensors and all numeric training metrics matched Round447 exactly. Run ID, checkpoint path, and wall-clock timestamp naturally differ. The full replay took 228.62 s, effectively identical to Round453’s 228.64 s; sample preparation took 163.68 s vs Round453’s 163.07 s, so this replay did not show an additional end-to-end speed gain from precomputing team signatures. It was 3.21% faster in sample preparation than Round447, but that comparison includes multiple changes and run-to-run timing variation.

public_mechanics_static_facts_benchmark.context: Round455 precomputes own Fake Out capability and format-specific learnability once per audited player-view record.
public_mechanics_static_facts_benchmark.scope_note: Encoder only; JSON parsing and the rest of transition extraction are excluded. Linear estimate is not end-to-end timing.

public_mechanics_static_facts_replay.context: Matched Round447 PPO replay: same audited data, initialization, seed, and 1,272 optimizer steps.
public_mechanics_static_facts_replay.finding: The public-mechanics static-facts cache reduced its isolated encoder median by 11.56% (48.27 to 42.69 ms) with exact feature parity. In the matched PPO replay, preparation took 161.79 s, 1.89 s lower than Round454 and 7.32 s below Round447. This is the fastest of the recent replay samples, but a single replay per code state cannot establish a stable speedup. Full update wall time from UTC start/completion timestamps rounded to seconds was about 224 s versus 228.6 s in Rounds453/454; do not treat this as a reliable end-to-end improvement. All 30 numeric metrics and all 82 model tensors matched Round447 exactly. Complete-iteration games/s remains 16.49 from Round430 because rollout generation was not measured here.
public_mechanics_static_facts_replay.scope_note: PPO update only; self-play rollout generation excluded. Wall time is rounded to whole UTC seconds from run-start and completion telemetry. Repeat matched replays to separate savings from run variation. Isolated public-mechanics timing excludes JSON parsing and other transition extraction.

audited_reader_validation_fastpath.context: Round457 uses NumPy finite checks for rectangular action-feature arrays and validates only agent-map fields present in each trajectory step.
audited_reader_validation_fastpath.scope_note: Includes offset reads, orjson decoding, and full row validation for a fixed prefix of audited records. Does not include transition extraction, model-input construction, or PPO optimization.

round456_public_mechanics_encoder.context: Public-mechanics encoder avoids repeated own-team Fake Out normalization and temporary padded row lists.

round457_replay.finding: Round457 sample preparation took 161.40 s, 3.15 s slower than Round456; full wall time was 226.59 s vs 223.76 s. These single-run comparisons do not show an end-to-end speed improvement from the map-field traversal change, despite a 6.0% audited reader microbenchmark reduction. All 28 numeric training metrics and all 82 model tensors matched Round447 bit-for-bit. Keep the simple validator fast paths as measured local reductions, but do not report a stable full-update speed gain; sample preparation remains the dominant cost. Complete-iteration throughput is still the historical 16.49 games/s Round430 result because no rollout occurred here.

round458_stage_profile.finding: Exact in-loop attribution identifies loading/parsing/validation as the largest stage, then transition extraction and input construction. A standalone full-reader measured 26.89 s and did not reproduce the 78.51 s in-loop row-loading bucket. All 28 numeric PPO metrics and all 82 model tensors matched Round447 exactly. No rollout was measured, so this is not a new games/s result.

opportunities.title: Profile the load path in place
opportunities.detail: Separate indexed seek/read, JSON decoding, strict validation, object allocation, and garbage collection inside full training chunks; the standalone reader missed most of the in-loop load cost.

opportunities.title: Shorten decoded-row lifetime
opportunities.detail: Stream validated transitions into compact arrays and release record dictionaries promptly; measure peak RSS and verify exact sample parity.

opportunities.title: Batch feature preparation
opportunities.detail: Vectorize transition extraction and model-input construction over contiguous arrays while retaining perspective-safe validation.

opportunities.title: Test bounded read prefetch
opportunities.detail: Only if CPU, storage, memory bandwidth, and GPU contention profiles support it; report memory and complete-update wall time.

round460_gc_profile.status: Two matched PPO-only runs reproduced the speed and exact parity; GC suppression is now default in the local CLI. Rollout-inclusive throughput remains unmeasured.
round460_gc_profile.finding: Across two matched GC-disabled PPO-only runs, mean wall time was 151.56 s (150.66–152.46) vs 227.17 s in Round458; mean preparation was 86.35 s (85.45–87.25) vs 162.08 s. Both runs matched all 28 numeric metrics and 82 tensors; peak RSS was about 7.32 GiB.
round460_gc_profile.rejected_round459: Disabling GC only during per-chunk record loading reduced the loader timer but total preparation increased to 171.74 s; GC work shifted into later feature-building stages.

round430_opening_intervention.summary: Replacing Round430 decisions 0–4 with public Max Damage actions improved all four main screens: on 512 matched clusters, +8.40 pp vs Max Damage, +7.13 vs public Counterplay, +8.50 vs Round464 PPO, and +10.64 vs Round465 PPO (95% cluster interval +6.64 to +14.65). Against historical PPO Round102, two disjoint 128-cluster sets gained +7.62 pp and +8.79 pp; pooled over 256 clusters the paired gain was +8.20 pp (95% interval +3.32 to +13.09). Exact team, preview, and battle-seed matching; no timeouts or action corrections. The prior reversed-orientation Round465 score was not complemented; a direct matched Round430 rerun supplies the raw score and paired result. This remains a Round430-specific heuristic intervention, not a learned-policy improvement. A smaller decision-1-and-4 hybrid transferred on 512 matched clusters: +4.88 pp vs Max Damage (+1.76 to +8.01), +4.00 vs public Counterplay (+0.88 to +7.13), +6.54 vs Round464 PPO (+3.52 to +9.67), and +7.42 vs Round465 PPO (+4.30 to +10.55). All four paired cluster intervals exclude zero on these samples; these are promising opening heuristics, not policy learning or established optimal play. Fresh-seed replication pooled across 640 disjoint team clusters confirmed +5.23 pp vs Max Damage (95% CI +2.50 to +7.97), +4.26 pp vs public Counterplay (+1.56 to +6.95), and +7.85 pp vs Round465 PPO (+5.20 to +10.59). Round464 also replicated independently. All four opponents now have pooled 640-cluster estimates; results remain Round430-specific heuristic evidence. Round464 pooled across both disjoint sets is +7.03 pp (95% CI +4.41 to +9.65).
